newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mixed, downtrend stalling.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mixed, downtrend stalling.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended mixed Friday, with the month-long downtrend stalling for now, but the longer term outlook remaining bearish, analysts said.

"The situation is deteriorating as the much delayed turn in economic activity in Europe and Japan has left the metals sector in surplus," Goldman Sachs commodities research director, Steve Strongin said.
"At current demand levels inventories are building, providing a growing cushion against new demand when it finally arrives," he said.
"Should economic growth in Europe and Japan falter once again, or should growth in those regions remain tepid, the outlook for metals will turn progressively more negative," he said.
But precious metals prices have recovered a little this week from a month long downtrend which took spot gold prices to 18 month lows at $376.90 an ounce, down from around $417.00 in February.
COMEX December gold ended down 10 cents at $382.60 an ounce, after trading up to $383.50 intraday.
In bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted around $380.25 compared to the London Friday afternoon fix at $380.70, and the New York close Thursday around $380.10.
COMEX December silver ended down 3.0 cents at $487.50 an ounce, after trading up to $4.935 intraday.

With the annual IMF/World Bank meeting over without further sign an imminent IMF gold sale, and with the Wilmington Trust's silver stocks now known, two bearish factors have been lifted, allowing precious metals prices to form a base near long term support levels, traders said.

Wilmington Trust becomes an official COMEX depositary from January 1, 1997 and reported eligible silver stocks of 59.4 million ounces this seek. Total COMEX silver stocks currently stand at 139,890,850 ounces.
The spot gold/silver ratio ended higher at 78.24, after declining in the past 10 days from an 18 month high of 78.55 on September 20.
Technically, on the daily charts, momentum indicators for precious metals have been showing some divergence from recent price downtrends, suggesting the downtrend may be bottoming, analysts noted.
NYMEX January 1997 platinum, now the active month with most open interest, ended up 50 cents an ounce at $388.00, while NYMEX December palladium closed up 40 cents at $121.60 an ounce.

Investor demand for precious metals is still seen limited by low inflation, and surging U.S. equity and debt markets, while industrial and investor demand in other countries has been restrained by a strong U.S. dollar pushing up the cost of precious metals in local currencies, analysts said.
In addition, further European central bank gold sales, which in the past have sometimes occurred late in the year, may again hang over the market in November, analysts said.

Some European central banks are expected to sell more gold as their reserves are expected to be surplus to requirements under the expected move to a single European currency managed by the European Monetary Institute from 1999, analysts said.
-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1641 email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
